title: Clause types and particles

objectives.can: Classify a clause as verbal, nominal or participial, and say what הִנֵּה, עַתָּה, גַּם, אַךְ, רַק, לָכֵן and עַל־כֵּן signal.

explanation.summary: Hebrew clauses come in a few shapes, and small particles tell the reader how one clause stands to another: look, now, also, only, therefore. This lesson names the shapes and the commonest of these particles, so that a verse can be read for its logic as well as its words.

sections.heading: Three shapes of clause
body: A verbal clause has a finite verb (a qatal, a yiqtol, a wayyiqtol and so on) as its predicate. A nominal clause has no verb: a noun, an adjective, a pronoun or a prepositional phrase is the predicate, as you saw in the lesson on nominal clauses.

A participial clause has a participle as its predicate. The participle is a verbal adjective, so it has no tense of its own. The time comes from the context: it may be the present, a continuing action in the past, or an action that is about to happen. Many grammars treat the participial clause as a kind of nominal clause, because it has no finite verb; others give it a class of its own. The labels differ, but the reading is the same.

The labels are tools for reading. A single sentence may join all three: a narrative chain of wayyiqtols can be interrupted by a nominal clause that describes the scene, and a speech may contain verbal, nominal and participial clauses side by side.

sections.heading: הִנֵּה: look, here is
body: הִנֵּה draws the hearer's attention to something. In speech it is often rendered 'behold' or 'look', but it is better understood as a pointer: what follows is presented as present, visible or about to happen. It stands at the head of a clause and is often followed by a subject and then a participle: that is how a participial clause is commonly introduced.
With a pronominal suffix it becomes a reply to a call. הִנְנִי and הִנֵּנִי mean 'here I am' (literally 'look, me'). The speaker presents himself as present and ready to answer.

When הִנֵּה begins a participial clause, the action it describes is often right now or imminent: the speaker announces what is on the point of happening. This is a tendency of the construction, not a rule that settles every verse.

sections.heading: עַתָּה and וְעַתָּה: now
body: עַתָּה is an adverb of time, 'now', and sometimes it is only that. But with the connecting וְ, וְעַתָּה often does not say when; it turns the argument. A speaker has described a situation, and וְעַתָּה brings the consequence: 'that being so, then …'. A command or request frequently follows, and the word stands close to our 'and so', 'now then'.
You have to decide in each verse whether the time or the logic is uppermost. Often both are present.

sections.heading: Therefore: לָכֵן and עַל כֵּן
body: Both words look back to what was said and say that something follows from it. לָכֵן is built from the preposition ל and the adverb כֵּן, 'so'. עַל כֵּן is two words, the preposition עַל and כֵּן, 'upon so', for this reason.

A common tendency is the following. לָכֵן more often introduces an announcement of what will happen, the consequence still ahead: in the prophets, a charge is followed by לָכֵן and then the sentence. עַל כֵּן more often explains why a situation already exists: why a place has its name, why a custom lasts, why something has happened. Both can, however, stand in other places, and in a given verse the choice is for the reader to weigh. Do not turn the tendency into a rule.

sections.heading: Adding and restricting
body: גַּם and אַף add: 'also', 'even', 'moreover'. They can join two clauses or point at a single word that is added to the others. In a series, a clause beginning with וְגַם tells the reader that another item or another fact is coming.

אַךְ and רַק restrict. They limit what has just been said or what is about to be said: 'only', 'except that', 'but', 'however'. A law or a speech often grants something in general and then restricts it with one of these words. Grammars also describe an affirming sense of אַךְ and רַק, 'surely, in truth', and the corpus marks both words as affirmative particles; in a given verse the restricting sense is the commoner one, but you must read the context.
The difference between אַךְ and רַק is slight. Many grammarians find no systematic difference of meaning between them; you will meet both, even in neighbouring clauses.

sections.heading: Questions with ה
body: A yes-or-no question usually begins with the prefix ה on the first word, pointed הֲ before most letters. The question has no other signal: the word order stays as in a statement. When ה is joined to the negative לֹא, as in הֲלֹא, the question usually expects the answer 'yes': 'Is it not so?' means 'It is so.' Many such questions are rhetorical: they make a point, and they are not asking for information.
Content questions use their own words (מִי, מָה, אַיֵּה and the like) and need no ה.

head: Word
What it tends to signal
Where it stands
rows: points at something present or about to happen; with a suffix, 'here I am'
head of a clause, often before a participle
time 'now', or the turn to a consequence
head of a clause, often before a command
therefore: more often an announcement of what follows
head of a clause, often after a charge
for this reason: more often an explanation of what already is

misunderstandings: הִנֵּה is not a verb and does not mean 'see!' as a command to the eye. It is a particle that presents what follows. With a suffix it is how Hebrew says 'here I am'.
וְעַתָּה does not always mean 'and now' in time. Often it turns from a situation to its consequence, and a command follows.
The difference between לָכֵן and עַל כֵּן is a tendency, not a law. Both can be rendered 'therefore'; read the verse before deciding which kind of 'therefore' it is.
A clause with a participle is not a past tense. The participle shows no time of its own; the context supplies it.

deeper.heading: A clause that is not what it seems
body: Grammarians disagree about where exactly to draw the line between nominal and verbal clauses. Some classify by the first word of the clause, so that a clause that begins with a noun counts as nominal even if a finite verb follows. Others classify by the predicate, so that only a clause with no verb is nominal. The account in this lesson follows the second view. The first view comes up again in the lessons on fronting and word order.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel is come unto Me; moreover I have seen the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three particles at work. וְעַתָּה turns from the story of Israel's suffering, which God has just told, to what follows from it. הִנֵּה presents the cry as something now arrived: the clause that follows has the cry as its subject and the verb בָּאָה, 'has come', as its predicate. וְגַם adds a second fact: 'and also I have seen'.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: thus saith the LORD: In this thou shalt know that I am the LORD — behold, I will smite with the rod that is in my hand upon the waters which are in the river, and they shall be turned to blood.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A participial clause with הִנֵּה. The subject is אָנֹכִי and the predicate is the participle מַכֶּה, 'striking'. There is no finite verb; the context makes it a near future: God announces what he is about to do with the rod.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Now therefore forgive, I pray thee, my sin only this once, and entreat the LORD your God, that He may take away from me this death only.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Pharaoh begins וְעַתָּה, 'now then', and an imperative follows. Both אַךְ and רַק restrict: the pardon is asked for 'only this once', and the death is the only thing to be taken away. The two words stand in the same sentence with the same restricting sense.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that come into Dagon's house, tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: עַל כֵּן explains a present custom. The verse comes after the story of how Dagon fell in front of the ark, and it says why the priests of Dagon still avoid the threshold 'to this day'. The reason lies in the past; the result is something that still goes on.

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: Therefore My people are gone into captivity, for want of knowledge; and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude are parched with thirst.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: לָכֵן follows a long charge against the people (the verses before it describe their conduct) and opens the sentence on them. Here it announces a consequence: the clause that follows says what befalls the people. The verb גָּלָה is a qatal; scholars read it as a certain future (a so-called prophetic perfect) or as a vivid way to describe what is already under way. The particle does not settle that question.

practice.prompt: What does the word וְגַם (word 14) do in this verse?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses, and He said: 'Is there not Aaron thy brother the Levite? I know that he can speak well. And also, behold, he cometh forth to meet thee; and when he seeth thee, he will be glad in his heart.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It asks a question
It draws a consequence from what was said before
It adds a further fact: 'and also, look, he is coming out'
It restricts what was said before
practice.explain: גַּם adds. God has just named Aaron; he adds that Aaron is already on his way. The next word, הִנֵּה, points at that fact as present.

practice.prompt: What does אַךְ־ (word 0) do at the head of this clause?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Only flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It asks a question
It adds a second permission
It marks a command
It restricts what was just permitted: 'only flesh with its life you shall not eat'
practice.explain: The verse before gives permission to eat every moving creature. אַךְ limits it: the blood is excepted. A restriction after a general grant is the typical place for אַךְ.

practice.prompt: What is Samuel saying with הִנֵּנִי (word 5)?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: that the LORD called Samuel; and he said: 'Here am I.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'Here I am': הִנֵּה with the suffix 'me' answers the call
'Behold, I am coming'
'Look at him'
'Do not call me'
practice.explain: הִנֵּה with a suffix presents the speaker himself. It is the Hebrew reply to a call: the one called says that he is present and ready.

practice.prompt: What kind of clause is the clause that begins with גָדוֹל (words 3 to 6), after 'I know that'?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods; yea, for that they dealt proudly against them.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A verbal clause with a qatal
A participial clause
A nominal clause: the adjective is the predicate and יְהוָה the subject
A question
practice.explain: There is no finite verb and no participle. The adjective גָדוֹל, 'great', comes first and is the predicate; the subject is יְהוָה; the phrase with מִכָּל says compared with whom.

practice.prompt: What does עַל כֵּן (words 15 and 16) do in this verse?

quoted.title: 1 Chronicles
quoted.english: So they came up to Baal-perazim, and David smote them there; and David said: 'God hath broken mine enemies by my hand, like the breach of waters.' Therefore they called the name of that place Baal-perazim.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It explains why the place has the name that follows, from the event just told
It introduces a question
It announces a future punishment
It restricts the earlier clause: 'only'
practice.explain: The story of David's victory is told, and עַל כֵּן gives the reason for a name that still stands. This explanatory use is the typical place for עַל כֵּן, though it is a tendency, not a rule.

check.prompt: What does וְעַתָּה (word 0) do at the head of this verse?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Now therefore go, and I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt speak.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It restricts the earlier statement
It asks a question
It turns from what was said to its consequence and introduces a command
It marks a past event
check.explain: Moses has objected that he cannot speak. God answers 'that being so' and gives the command לֵךְ, 'go'. The word is used to move from a situation to what must be done about it, more than to mark time.

check.prompt: What do אַךְ (word 4) and רַק (word 11) have in common here?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Now therefore forgive, I pray thee, my sin only this once, and entreat the LORD your God, that He may take away from me this death only.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Both ask a question
Both add a further request
Both restrict the request, 'only this once' and 'only this death'
One is a verb and the other a noun
check.explain: Both limit what Pharaoh asks. The two particles stand in one sentence with no difference of sense that a reader can point to, which is why many grammarians treat them as near equivalents.

check.prompt: What does לָכֵן (word 0) signal at the head of this verse?

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: Therefore My people are gone into captivity, for want of knowledge; and their honourable men are famished, and their multitude are parched with thirst.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It repeats the charge of the verse before
It begins a question
It marks a command
It announces the consequence of the charge made earlier: a judgment follows
check.explain: In the prophets, לָכֵן commonly follows a charge and introduces the sentence upon those charged. This is a tendency; the same word elsewhere introduces other results.

check.prompt: What does עַל כֵּן (words 0 and 1) do in this verse?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that come into Dagon's house, tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It restricts the custom to one place
It explains why a custom still holds, from an event told earlier
It asks why
It announces a punishment still to come
check.explain: The priests avoid the threshold 'to this day'. The reason is the earlier event. This is the explanatory use of עַל כֵּן.

check.prompt: What does אַף־ (word 2) do in this verse?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: these also are accounted Rephaim, as the Anakim; but the Moabites call them Emim.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It adds the people named to those already counted: 'these also'
It restricts the clause: 'only'
It is the noun 'anger'
It marks a command
check.explain: The verse puts the Emim beside the Rephaim: they too are counted in that group. אַף here adds. (The same letters can be a noun meaning 'nose' or 'anger'; the context decides.)

check.prompt: What kind of clause is הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי הֹרֵג (words 8 to 10)?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And I have said unto thee: Let My son go, that he may serve Me; and thou hast refused to let him go. Behold, I will slay thy son, thy first-born.' —
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A nominal clause with a noun as predicate
A verbal clause with a qatal
A participial clause: the participle הֹרֵג is the predicate and אָנֹכִי its subject
A verbal clause with a yiqtol
check.explain: The participle is the only verbal element, and it has no finite form. The context gives the time: the act is about to be done. Some grammars would call the clause nominal because there is no finite verb.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And the LORD called yet again Samuel. And Samuel arose and went to Eli, and said: 'Here am I; for thou didst call me.' And he answered: 'I called not, my son; lie down again.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'Here I am': הִנֵּה with the suffix 'me'
'Behold, you called': a past tense
'Do not call me': a negative command
'They are here': הִנֵּה with a plural suffix
check.explain: The suffix on הִנֵּה is 'me'. The speaker presents himself in answer to the call, as in the other verses of the story.

check.prompt: What does the question word הֲלֹא (word 0) expect as its answer?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Said he not himself unto me: She is my sister? and she, even she herself said: He is my brother. In the simplicity of my heart and the innocency of my hands have I done this.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'Yes': the question says, 'Did he not say it?'
'No': the question denies it
No answer at all
A name or a place
check.explain: הֲלֹא is the question prefix ה joined to the negative לֹא. Such a question usually expects the answer 'yes' and is often rhetorical. Abimelech is saying, in effect, 'He did say it.'

check.prompt: What does אַךְ (word 0) do in this verse of laws?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.english: Nevertheless these ye shall not eat of them that only chew the cud, or of them that only have the hoof cloven: the camel, and the hare, and the rock-badger, because they chew the cud but part not the hoof, they are unclean unto you;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It adds another animal that may be eaten
It gives the reason for the law
It restricts what the verse before allowed: 'only these you shall not eat'
It marks a question
check.explain: The verse before allows the eating of animals that chew the cud and have a divided hoof. אַךְ limits that permission by naming exceptions. The reason follows later, with כִּי.

check.prompt: What kind of clause is הִנֵּה יֹצֵא הַמַּיְמָה (words 4 to 6)?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Get thee unto Pharaoh in the morning; lo, he goeth out unto the water; and thou shalt stand by the river's brink to meet him; and the rod which was turned to a serpent shalt thou take in thy hand.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A question
A verbal clause with a yiqtol
A participial clause: יֹצֵא is the predicate, and the time is the moment of speaking
A nominal clause with a noun as predicate
check.explain: The participle יֹצֵא, 'going out', follows הִנֵּה, and the subject is not written: it is Pharaoh, named in the command before. The time is set by the context: he is going out now, and Moses is to meet him.

check.prompt: What does עַל כֵּן (words 19 and 20) do here?

quoted.title: 1 Kings
quoted.english: they shall be answered: Because they forsook the LORD their God, who brought forth their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods, and worshipped them, and served them; therefore hath the LORD brought all this evil upon them.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It introduces the consequence of the reasons just given: because they left the LORD, for this reason he brought the evil
It marks a command
It restricts the earlier statement
It asks for the reason
check.explain: The reasons stand first, in the clauses with עַל אֲשֶׁר. Then עַל כֵּן links them to what happened. The event is already accomplished (the verb is a qatal), so the sentence explains a situation that exists rather than announcing one still to come.

reading.why: God's address to Moses uses the particles of this lesson in sequence: וְעַתָּה, הִנֵּה, וְגַם, a second וְעַתָּה with a command, and Moses's answer with הִנֵּה and a participle. The verses show how the particles carry the argument from the situation to the task.

segments.title: Exodus
segments.english: And now, behold, the cry of the children of Israel is come unto Me; moreover I have seen the oppression wherewith the Egyptians oppress them.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Exodus
segments.english: Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth My people the children of Israel out of Egypt.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Exodus
segments.english: And Moses said unto God: 'Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Exodus
segments.english: And He said: 'Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be the token unto thee, that I have sent thee: when thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Exodus
segments.english: And Moses said unto God: 'Behold, when I come unto the children of Israel, and shall say unto them: The God of your fathers hath sent me unto you; and they shall say to me: What is His name? what shall I say unto them?'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)
